systemPrompt: You are the documentation assistant for umarag, a client-side RAG SDK that runs retrieval and LLM inference entirely in the browser. Answer ONLY using the provided context. If the answer isn't in the context, say you don't know and point the user to the project README. Never invent APIs, config fields, or model names. Cite the context entry you used with [n].

chunks.text: EdgeChatConfig fields: knowledgeUrl (required): URL of the knowledge export JSON. systemPrompt: overrides the export's baked-in system prompt. topK: number of chunks retrieved per query, default 4. minScore: minimum cosine similarity for a chunk to be retrieved, default 0 — retrieval is top-K only unless you raise it; note that question-to-paragraph scores commonly sit between 0.2 and 0.45, so high cutoffs silently empty results. engine: 'auto' | 'webllm' | 'prompt-api', default 'auto'. webllmModel: WebLLM model id, default 'Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-q4f16_1-MLC'. webllmAppConfig: a custom WebLLM model registry for self-hosted weights. onProgress: callback receiving `{ text, progress }` reports during loading.

Engine selection: With engine 'auto' (the default), umarag prefers WebLLM when webllmModel or webllmAppConfig is configured — you picked that model deliberately — and otherwise prefers the browser's built-in Prompt API, falling back to the other engine when the preferred one can't run. Force engine: 'webllm' or 'prompt-api' to pin one. If no engine can run, init() throws EdgeChatUnsupportedError naming both reasons.

Compatibility and engine switching: checkCompatibility() reports — without loading any model — whether each engine can run on the current device: `{ webllm: { supported, reason? }, promptApi: { supported, reason? }, shaderF16 }`. The reason field explains why a backend can't run (e.g. no WebGPU adapter, Prompt API absent). shaderF16 is true when the GPU supports half-precision shaders — pick a q4f16 model build when true, q4f32 otherwise. switchEngine(kind) swaps the LLM engine on a live EdgeChat instance without reloading the knowledge base or embedder, and returns the engine now active; the new engine is initialized before the old one is released, so a failed switch keeps the current engine working.

Guardrails and system prompt: The retrieved chunks are injected as numbered context entries into a system message. The default guardrail instructs the model to answer only from that context, admit when the answer isn't there, and cite sources with [n] notation. Ship your own guardrail by baking systemPrompt into the knowledge export at build time, or override it at runtime with the systemPrompt config field — the runtime field wins.

Error types: EdgeChatUnsupportedError: no usable engine on this device (no WebGPU adapter and no Prompt API). EdgeChatSchemaVersionError: the knowledge export's schemaVersion doesn't match what this client supports (currently 1). EdgeChatEmbeddingMismatchError: the query embedding dimension differs from the export's embeddingDim — your export and runtime embedding model are out of sync. A non-OK HTTP response for the export throws a plain Error naming the URL and status code.

How this demo is served: The demo is a Vite + React app built to static files and served by a plain Python http.server on 127.0.0.1:8787, exposed to the private tailnet over HTTPS with `tailscale serve --bg --https=10000 8787`. Tailscale provides valid TLS certificates for the tailnet hostname, which matters because WebGPU only works in secure contexts. Any device joining the tailnet — Mac, Windows, Linux, Android, iPhone — can open the demo URL and run the full RAG stack in its own browser.

Model files on disk: The Gemma weights live in the examples/react-demo/models/ directory (both q4f16 and q4f32 builds plus their compiled wasm libs) and are symlinked into dist/ after each build with `ln -sfn ../models dist/models`, since vite build wipes dist. They were downloaded once from HuggingFace with curl against resolve/main URLs and size-verified against the repo manifest.

Rebuilding the demo: From examples/react-demo: `bun install`, then `bun run build-kb` to regenerate the knowledge export from the markdown files in docs/, then `bun run build`, then recreate the models symlink. If the umarag SDK source changed, run `npm run build` at the repo root first — the demo consumes the SDK via a local file: link.

Installation: Install the package and its peer dependencies: `npm install @sa4drao/umarag @orama/orama @huggingface/transformers`. If you want the WebLLM engine (recommended unless you only target Chrome's built-in Prompt API), also install `@mlc-ai/web-llm` — it is an optional peer dependency and is only dynamically imported when the WebLLM engine is actually selected. Node 18+ is required for tooling; the runtime itself is browser-only ESM.

Minimal usage: Create an EdgeChat with the URL of your knowledge export, call init(), then ask() or stream(). Example: `const chat = new EdgeChat({ knowledgeUrl: "/kb-export.json" }); await chat.init(); const { sources, stream } = await chat.stream("How do I authenticate?", history); for await (const delta of stream) { ui.append(delta); }`. ask() returns the full `{ answer, sources }` once; stream() resolves with the retrieved sources up front plus an async generator of answer deltas.

Conversational memory: Both ask() and stream() take prior turns as an optional second argument: an array of { role, content } ChatMessage objects, oldest first, without the current query. Keep your own turn list and pass it back on every call — that is the assistant's memory. The most recent eight turns are included in the prompt so small on-device context windows don't overflow. Both methods call init() implicitly if you forget.

Lifecycle: init() is idempotent while in flight and after success — concurrent callers share one promise. A failed init() is NOT cached: calling init() again retries the whole pipeline, so a transient network failure doesn't brick the instance. When you're done (e.g. a SPA route unmount), call dispose() to release GPU memory held by the LLM engine, the embedding pipeline, and the index. A disposed instance can be re-init()ed.

Progress reporting: Pass onProgress to the config to drive a loading UI. umarag reports coarse phases ("Loading knowledge base…", "Loading embedding model…") with progress 0, and WebLLM reports granular download/compile progress with text and a 0–1 progress fraction. Chrome's built-in model reports "Downloading built-in model…" when the Prompt API needs to fetch its model first.

Schema: The knowledge export is a JSON file with schemaVersion (currently 1), embeddingModel (the transformers.js model id used to embed the chunks, e.g. "Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"), embeddingDim (vector dimension, 384 for MiniLM), an optional systemPrompt (the shipped guardrail), and chunks — an array of `{ id, text, embedding, metadata? }` objects where embedding is a plain number array. The same model named in embeddingModel is loaded in the browser to embed queries, so the two always stay in sync; a dimension mismatch throws EdgeChatEmbeddingMismatchError.

Producing an export: umarag consumes exports, it does not produce them — your build pipeline does. Any process that can run an embedding model works. The demo's scripts/build-kb.ts is one concrete example: it reads the markdown files in docs/, splits them into per-heading chunks, embeds each chunk with MiniLM via transformers.js in Node, and writes public/kb-export.json. Re-run it whenever the docs change. Chunk ids look like "configuration#engine-selection" so cited sources point back to the exact doc section.

Scale limits: Retrieval is exact brute-force cosine similarity over an in-memory Orama index — fast at hundreds to low thousands of chunks, which covers most product-docs use cases. If your knowledge base is much larger, pre-filter or shard the export (for example one export per product area) rather than shipping everything to every browser tab.

What is umarag?: umarag (@sa4drao/umarag) is a client-side RAG chatbot runtime: retrieval and LLM inference both run in the browser, with zero backend at query time. You ship a static vector export produced by your own pipeline; umarag fetches it, builds an in-memory vector index with Orama, embeds queries with transformers.js, and generates grounded answers with an on-device LLM — either WebLLM over WebGPU or the browser's built-in Prompt API. No inference server, no API keys, no per-token bill, and no user data ever leaves the tab.

Architecture: At init, umarag fetches the knowledge export (a JSON file from any static host), validates its schema version, and inserts the pre-computed chunk embeddings into an Orama vector index. It then loads the embedding model named in the export via transformers.js (WebGPU with automatic wasm fallback) and selects an LLM engine. At query time, the user's question is embedded on-device, the top-K most similar chunks are retrieved by cosine similarity, and a system prompt containing those chunks as numbered context is sent to the on-device LLM, which streams the answer token by token.

The three things a team ships: umarag is designed around handing off exactly three artifacts: Guardrails (a system prompt baked into the export that pins the assistant to your docs), a Model (a WebLLM model id, optionally self-hosted weights, or the browser's built-in model), and Embeddings (the knowledge export JSON produced by your build pipeline). Everything is static files — nothing to operate.

Project status: umarag is at version 0.4.0, pre-release, not yet published to npm. It is MIT licensed. The 0.2 release added self-hosted model weights via webllmAppConfig, retryable initialization, phase-level progress reporting, session cleanup for the Prompt API engine, and a dispose() method that releases GPU memory. The 0.3 release added checkCompatibility() for probing which engines a device can run, switchEngine() for swapping the LLM engine on a live instance without reloading the knowledge base, and smarter 'auto' engine selection that prefers a deliberately configured WebLLM model. The 0.4 release added conversational memory (a history parameter on ask() and stream(), honored by both engines), a stream() shape that returns the retrieved sources once up front, lazy loading of transformers.js for leaner initial bundles, and stricter validation of the knowledge export.

Why self-host: By default WebLLM downloads model weights from HuggingFace. Passing webllmAppConfig lets you serve the weights from your own origin instead — useful for air-gapped networks, private tailnets, faster LAN loads, and guaranteeing exactly which model binary runs. The demo you are reading this in serves Gemma 2 2B from the same machine that hosts the page; no model CDN is involved at load time.

Directory layout and the resolve/main rule: Mirror the HuggingFace layout on disk: the weight files (mlc-chat-config.json, ndarray-cache.json, params_shard_*.bin, tokenizer files) must live under `<model-id>/resolve/main/`, and the model URL in webllmAppConfig must end with a slash. This is because WebLLM appends "resolve/main/" to any model URL that doesn't already contain a "/resolve/<revision>/" segment. The model_lib field points to the compiled WebGPU wasm for the model architecture — it must come from the binary-mlc-llm-libs release matching your installed @mlc-ai/web-llm version (for 0.2.84: web-llm-models/v0_2_84/base/).

Example config: `webllmAppConfig: { model_list: [{ model: location.origin + "/models/gemma-2-2b-it-q4f16_1-MLC/resolve/main/", model_id: "gemma-2-2b-it-q4f16_1-MLC", model_lib: location.origin + "/models/gemma-2-2b-it-q4f16_1_cs1k-webgpu.wasm" }] }` — pass it together with webllmModel set to the same model_id and engine set to 'webllm'.

Picking a quantization per device: The q4f16 build (~1.4 GB) requires the GPU to expose the shader-f16 WebGPU feature; the q4f32 build (same weights, also ~1.4 GB on disk, more VRAM at runtime) runs everywhere WebGPU does. The demo hosts both and probes `(await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter()).features.has("shader-f16")` at load time to pick — copy that pattern for maximum device coverage. Gemma 2 2B q4f16 needs roughly 1.9 GB of GPU memory, q4f32 roughly 2.5 GB.

Which models can run: Any model in WebLLM's prebuilt registry works out of the box (Llama 3.x, Gemma 2, Gemma 3 1B, Phi, Qwen, Mistral families). A model only runs if a compiled WebGPU wasm exists for its architecture in your WebLLM version — that is why Gemma 3n E2B and other very new architectures are not available: no MLC-compiled build exists for them yet. For small on-device use, gemma-2-2b-it (2B-class) is the workhorse and gemma-3-1b-it (~700 MB) is the light option for weaker phones.

WebGPU requirements per platform: umarag's WebLLM engine requires WebGPU; there is deliberately no CPU fallback because CPU inference of a 1B+ model in a browser is too slow to be a usable product. WebGPU ships by default in Chrome and Edge on Windows and macOS (since Chrome 113), in Chrome on Android for qualified devices (since Chrome 121), and in Safari on macOS, iOS, iPadOS and visionOS since Safari 26 / iOS 26. On Linux, Chrome needs chrome://flags/#enable-unsafe-webgpu and chrome://flags/#enable-vulkan enabled, then a relaunch.

GPU blocklist: adapter is null even though chrome://gpu says enabled: chrome://gpu can report "WebGPU: Hardware accelerated" while web pages still get null from navigator.gpu.requestAdapter() — Chrome keeps a blocklist of GPU/driver combinations for page-level access. The fix is enabling chrome://flags/#enable-unsafe-webgpu and relaunching Chrome. This is common on Android devices that are not in Chrome's qualified list. umarag surfaces this case as EdgeChatUnsupportedError with a "no adapter granted" message.

iPhone and iPad: WebGPU is available from iOS/iPadOS 26 onward — update the OS if the demo reports no adapter. Note that every browser on iOS (including Chrome and Firefox) is WebKit underneath outside the EU, so updating iOS, not the browser app, is what matters. The Prompt API (Gemini Nano) does not exist on iOS; WebGPU is the only engine path there.

shader-f16 missing: If the adapter exists but lacks the shader-f16 feature, a q4f16 model will refuse to load. Use the q4f32 build of the same model, or probe the adapter first and pick the right variant. The demo ships a /gpu-check.html page that prints the adapter name, shader-f16 support, and buffer limits for any device — open it on a failing device to see exactly what it supports.

First load is slow: The first load streams the model weights (~1.4 GB for Gemma 2 2B) and caches them in browser storage; subsequent loads read from cache and take seconds. The embedding model (~25 MB) is fetched from the HuggingFace CDN on first use and also cached. If loading stalls mid-way, a retry resumes safely — init() failures are not cached.
